candidate.blueprint_locator: Reduction of Risk Potential — monitor diagnostic data and client response, recognize inaccurate/abnormal monitoring information, and use monitoring technology safely
candidate.blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — continuous glucose monitoring / safe interpretation of monitoring data
candidate.educational_objective: Explain that CGMs measure interstitial glucose and provide trends/alerts, while confirmatory fingerstick or calibration requirements depend on the specific device and clinical situation.

options.A: A CGM sensor measures glucose in interstitial fluid and provides glucose values and trends; follow the specific device instructions for when meter confirmation or calibration is needed
options.B: A CGM measures venous blood glucose continuously through the sensor and completely replaces all other glucose testing for every device
options.C: A CGM provides only one glucose value each day and cannot display trends or alerts
options.D: CGM values are unrelated to glucose management and are used only to document exercise

candidate.rationale: FDA-cleared CGM systems use a sensor to measure glucose in interstitial fluid and can provide repeated/real-time glucose values, trends, and alerts that support diabetes management. Requirements for calibration or confirmatory fingerstick testing are device-specific, so a nurse should not teach that every CGM universally eliminates blood glucose meter use. FDA also advises meter confirmation when a sensor reading is suspected to be inaccurate or does not match symptoms. Therefore A is the best answer.
candidate.source_claim_supported: CGMs measure interstitial glucose and provide ongoing values/trends/alerts; blood-glucose meter confirmation/calibration needs are device- and situation-specific rather than universally eliminated.

candidate.stem: A client with diabetes says, 'My continuous glucose monitor measures glucose directly from my blood, so I would never need a blood glucose meter.' Which response by the nurse is most accurate?
